near_miss.lead: ON um morgininn er lýsa tók ~ Arm. i cagel lowsoyn 'at daybreak' (lýsa ~ loys, *lewk-)
near_miss.why_not: Generic narrative time-marker after a night battle; only one cognate (light), different syntax (verb vs noun); no figure.

near_miss.lead: '(took a) wife who was named X, daughter of king Y' (nefna/heita + dóttir ~ θυγάτηρ τῇ οὔνομα ἦν; жена, дочь Микулична)
near_miss.why_not: Genealogical prose formula built from kin terms and 'name' that any tradition produces; the Greek uses dative-of-possessor ὄνομα, ON a participle nefnd/hét: no shared syntax beyond the universal.

near_miss.lead: mara trað hann (nightmare trod him) ~ Russ. ne velela s muzhem spat'
exposure of the king's corpse: létu rífa dýr ok fugla hræin (beasts and birds tear the corpse), cf. Homeric κύνεσσιν οἰωνοῖσί τε (Il. 1.4-5, recalled)
near_miss.why_not: No partner in slab carries the motif; the Homeric/OE 'beasts of battle' pairs are not cognate with dýr/fugl (renewal at best), so only a motif, not wording. Note hræ < *krewh2- (cf. Skt kravíṣ-, kravyā́d-) as possible lexical lead, not tested to a phrase.

near_miss.lead: glóða garmr ... beit (the hound of embers = fire bit [the king]) ~ fire as devouring animal
near_miss.why_not: Partners joined only by a spurious *ger mapping (garmr ~ jāla); fire-as-biter is a kenning motif, no cognate wording.

near_miss.lead: bera vitni (bear witness) ~ Lat. ferre (pacem fero; ferunt)
near_miss.why_not: Latin partners do not use fero with a 'witness' object; testimonium ferre not in slab; the ON law collocation is plausibly Latin-influenced legal idiom anyway.
Spurious: ON form is lǫg 'laws' (setti lǫg), not laug 'bath' (see error line).

near_miss.lead: stranger's identity: Ir. ní fes ainm ná máthair ná athair dó ~ Od. εἴπ' ὄνομ' ὅττι σε κεῖθι κάλεον μήτηρ τε πατήρ τε (ainm ~ ὄνομα, máthair ~ μήτηρ, athair ~ πατήρ)
near_miss.why_not: Three exact cognates in a congruent scene (asking a stranger's name), but the corpus search (name+mother+father within 8 words) returns many unrelated Greek, Irish and German hits (genealogies, NT, hagiography); the combination is the universal way to identify a person, and the Irish is a negative 'unknown' statement, the Greek a request. Not distinguishable from chance/generic.

near_miss.lead: kin list faðir, móðir, dóttir, systir, kona ~ сестры, матере, жены
near_miss.why_not: List of kin terms in a law of killing vs a chronicle list of women brought; kin lists are generic and the contexts differ.

near_miss.lead: horse stumbles, king falls head on stone, skull breaks and brain lies on the stone (cf. Homeric ἐγκέφαλος ... πεπάλακτο, recalled)
near_miss.why_not: Latin partner shares only caput/pedes body terms; the brain-spatter motif has no cognate wording (heili vs ἐγκέφαλος).

near_miss.lead: night/sleep: um nóttina ... svefn- ~ ἀΰπνους νύκτας
near_miss.why_not: Fjǫlnir drunk and sleepy at night vs Homeric 'sleepless nights': shared roots only, opposite sense, no figure.

near_miss.lead: maiden pours the king a vessel full of mead (byrlaði konungi ker fullt mjaðar)
near_miss.why_not: Greek partners irrelevant; best partners are outside the slab (see search lead).
ON law fines / carrying off a farmer's goods vs AV wealth prayers: single shared word, generic.

near_miss.lead: parental love: móðir hans unni honum mikit en faðir hans minna ~ mātṛ-vartī pitṛ-priyaḥ (dear to the father)
near_miss.why_not: Kin terms are cognate but the verbs are not (unna vs priya-; ON fríðr < *preyH- occurs in another clause); ON contrasts mother's love with father's lack of it, opposite of the Sanskrit: generic.

search_lead.cognate: ON fullr ~ OIr lán ~ Ved pūrṇá- (*pl̥h₁-nó-); ON mjǫðr (gen. mjaðar) ~ OIr mid ~ Ved mádhu- (*médʰu)
search_lead.argument: In the pivot Snæfríðr, a Finnish sorcerer's daughter, pours King Haraldr 'a vessel full of mead' and he is at once enthralled. In the Acallam (G303000) a maiden takes a silver cup from her bosom 'its fill of mead in it' and puts it in Finn's hand; in the Early Modern Irish parallel a horn 'its fill of mead' is put in the speaker's hand. In Eddic poetry Gerðr (Skm 37) and Sif (Ls 53) offer a cup 'full of old mead'. So a woman (often otherworldly) handing a man a vessel full of mead is common to Norse and Irish, with both nouns exact cognates; the Vedic 'full of mádhu' shows the collocation itself is old, though there in other contexts (Viṣṇu's steps, Indra's trough). Caveats: 'full of mead' is a natural collocation, and the Irish 'lán do' construction is a partitive noun phrase, not an adjective with genitive; the sovereignty-drink parallel (woman serving drink to the king, Irish flaith/laith) is recalled from the literature.
